newsitem.title: UK: ACPC to address arabica prices at London talks.
newsitem.headline: ACPC to address arabica prices at London talks.

text.p: The Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) technical group meets in London on Thursday to study the recent surge in coffee prices, which key member Colombia termed as "excessive", and its impact on consumption.
The group, which also comprises Brazil, El Salvador, Indonesia, Ivory Coast and Uganda, could draw up steps to tackle the price escalation and ensure a steady supply pipeline, ACPC officials said.
Traders expect no major decision at the group meeting. Members will have to report their findings and any necessary measures to the full ACPC council which is not expected to meet until May.
Delegates said the meeting is expected to address the surge in arabica coffee prices which producers feared could pose a threat to consumption in the longer-term.
New York's May arabica futures hit the $2.00 a lb mark on March 5 for the first time since the last major Brazilian frost. Prices have started to come down this week to trade at $1.68 on Tuesday.
Colombia's Finance Minister has called the $2.00 level excessive, a sentiment echoed elsewhere in the producing community.
A similar price rise occured in 1994, causing a slight drop in coffee consumption as people switched to cheaper beverages.
Prices of arabica, the premium coffee, has almost doubled between early December and early March this year. At the same time, robustas rose only by 50 percent.
"We don't want (high prices) to hit consumption levels," ACPC secretary-general Robeiro Oliveira Silva told Reuters last week.
But Silva added that although producers were keen to reduce the tightness in the supply of arabica coffee, they were concerned about the large discount at which robusta coffee is trading to arabica.
Silva did not elaborate on ways to reduce the tightness of arabica supplies.
Producer sources said Colombia, which requested the meeting, was perhaps spearheading a move to boost the supply of arabica coffee to the market.
"It would make sense for Colombia to do so as prices are good and they have stocks," said a senior trader.
The only reserves left for the free world at the moment are held by the Colombian Coffee Federation at six million bags and the Brazilian government (13.2 million).

Top ACPC member Brazil would not discuss the government's position before the meeting. In the case of Brazil, there is a growing feeling that the country will not be able to export any more than its current quota given domestic availability.

The ACPC council decided in Rio de Janeiro in January to cut a further 1.3 million 60-kg bags of coffee from exports in the first six months of this year. Robusta exports will be cut by 1.0 million bags and the remaining 300,000 bags will be arabicas.
The new cut of 1.3 million bags took projected exports by the 14-member group down to 24.98 million in the first half of 1997.
While the ACPC considers the interest of arabica producers, it will also have to weigh the concerns of producers of robusta, which saw price discount to arabica widening to an all-time-low.

Ivorian Commodities Minister Guy-Alain Gauze, who had spearheaded the idea of an extra cut in robusta exports, last week met ACPC President Rubens Barbosa of Brazil and agreed that the additional cuts agreed in Rio should be implemented "without any adjustments."
"We still have plenty of room (for price increase) in the case of robusta," ACPC's Silva said.
Indonesia, the world's largest robusta grower, has said that it would be timely for the ACPC to demonstrate it was not a cartel by considering the interests of consumers.
